passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — those peremptory norms of international law from which no derogation is permitted, even by treaty — has long occupied an uneasy position at the intersection of customary international law and the voluntary consent-based framework that underlies the international legal order. Unlike ordinary customary norms, which may be displaced by subsequent treaty arrangements between consenting states, jus cogens norms are held to be hierarchically superior: a treaty provision that conflicts with such a norm is void ab initio, regardless of the parties' expressed intentions. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, concluded in 1969, gave formal textual recognition to this hierarchy, yet it conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms had attained peremptory status, leaving that determination to state practice, opinio juris, and — increasingly — the pronouncements of international tribunals.

The indeterminacy inherent in this arrangement has generated persistent doctrinal controversy. Proponents of a robust jus cogens catalogue argue that the norms against genocide, torture, and slavery have so thoroughly permeated domestic and international legal systems that their peremptory character is beyond serious dispute; on this view, the very universality of their prohibition is itself the marker of their elevated status. Critics, however, contend that treating any norm as non-derogable risks calcifying international law at a particular historical moment, preventing the adaptive evolution that gives the international legal order its resilience. This tension is further complicated by the emergence of lex specialis principles: where a specialized treaty regime purports to displace a general norm within a defined domain — as when certain humanitarian law conventions specify permissible conduct in armed conflict that might otherwise appear to violate general prohibitions — courts must determine whether the specialized norm merely elaborates, or actually displaces, the background peremptory standard. Regrettably, international tribunals have not applied a consistent methodology in making this determination.

A further difficulty arises from the interaction of jus cogens with the domestic law of sovereign states. Where a state's constitutional order grants international treaty obligations the force of domestic law, a finding that a given treaty is void under jus cogens creates a legal lacuna: the treaty obligation cannot be enforced domestically, yet the constitutional provision that would have incorporated it remains operative. National courts in several civil-law jurisdictions — confronting precisely this predicament following the invalidation of certain bilateral investment agreements in 2017 — responded by applying residual common-law analogues to fill the gap, a solution that raises its own concerns about the legitimacy of judicial gap-filling in a domain traditionally reserved for state negotiation. One hopes that the International Law Commission's ongoing codification project will supply the clearer hierarchical rules that tribunals and domestic courts alike have long required, though the Commission's past practice of cataloguing rather than adjudicating contested norms suggests that definitive resolution may remain elusive.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate peremptory norms has rendered jus cogens an unworkable concept that international tribunals should abandon in favor of ordinary customary law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens, though formally recognized in international law, is beset by unresolved difficulties of identification, application, and interaction with domestic legal orders, leaving courts without reliable guidance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conflict between jus cogens norms and lex specialis principles represents the central crisis in contemporary international law and demands an urgent legislative response.

choices.label: D
choices.text: National courts have generally handled jus cogens conflicts more satisfactorily than international tribunals because domestic constitutional frameworks supply clearer hierarchical rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The International Law Commission's codification project offers the most promising avenue for resolving the longstanding controversies surrounding peremptory norms in international law.

explanations.correct: The passage traces three distinct layers of difficulty with jus cogens — its indeterminate identification (paragraph 1–2), its conflict with lex specialis (paragraph 2), and its disruptive interaction with domestic constitutional orders (paragraph 3) — and closes by doubting whether any resolution is imminent. B integrates all three strands without overstating or narrowing.
explanations.A: Too strong and wrong in direction — the author does not recommend abandoning jus cogens, only notes the difficulties it generates.
explanations.C: Too narrow — the lex specialis tension is one of several difficulties; the passage does not identify it as 'the central crisis' or call urgently for legislation.
explanations.D: Contradicted by the passage, which criticizes domestic courts' gap-filling as raising 'its own concerns about legitimacy.'
explanations.E: This restates only the closing suggestion, which the author immediately qualifies with skepticism — a classic 'restates a suggestion as the main point' trap.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined and its formal recognition described; two opposing theoretical positions on the doctrine's scope are presented; the doctrine's disruptive effect on domestic legal orders is examined; and a tentative remedy is proposed and immediately qualified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a historical controversy over its origins is traced; the doctrine's recent rejection by international tribunals is documented; and alternative frameworks are evaluated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An international legal principle is introduced; its consistent application across multiple jurisdictions is surveyed; a single anomalous case is examined; and the principle's overall effectiveness is affirmed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrinal tension is identified; the positions of proponents and critics are compared; an illustrative case study from domestic courts is introduced; and the doctrine is ultimately endorsed as coherent despite its difficulties.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A definition of a legal norm is offered; the norm's interaction with domestic constitutional law is traced historically; international tribunals' responses are catalogued; and a legislative reform is recommended.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines jus cogens and notes its formal recognition via the Vienna Convention. Paragraph 2 presents the proponent/critic debate and introduces the lex specialis complication. Paragraph 3 examines disruption to domestic legal orders via the 2017 investment agreement example. The final sentence proposes the ILC remedy while qualifying its likely efficacy. A tracks all four moves accurately.
explanations.B: Mis-describes the second paragraph as tracing 'origins controversy' and the third as 'rejection by tribunals' — neither is accurate.
explanations.C: Claims 'consistent application' and 'effectiveness affirmed,' both contradicted by the passage's critical thrust.
explanations.D: Claims the doctrine is 'ultimately endorsed as coherent' — the author reaches no such conclusion; the closing is skeptical.
explanations.E: Describes a historical trace and a legislative recommendation, neither of which the passage performs; the ILC project is mentioned as an uncertain hope, not a recommendation.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what feature distinguishes jus cogens norms from ordinary norms of customary international law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jus cogens norms are codified in a comprehensive enumerated list maintained by the International Law Commission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jus cogens norms may be displaced by subsequent treaties concluded between consenting states, while ordinary customary norms may not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jus cogens norms are hierarchically superior and cannot be derogated from even by treaty, whereas ordinary customary norms may be displaced by such agreements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jus cogens norms derive their authority exclusively from the consent of sovereign states, unlike ordinary customary norms, which arise from state practice alone.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jus cogens norms are enforced directly by domestic courts, while ordinary customary norms are enforceable only through international tribunals.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly: 'Unlike ordinary customary norms, which may be displaced by subsequent treaty arrangements between consenting states, jus cogens norms are held to be hierarchically superior.' C paraphrases this distinction accurately.
explanations.A: Contradicted by the passage, which notes the Vienna Convention 'conspicuously declined to enumerate' such norms.
explanations.B: This inverts the distinction described in the passage.
explanations.D: Reverses the consent-based logic — the passage describes ordinary customary law as operating within the 'voluntary consent-based framework,' not jus cogens.
explanations.E: The passage makes no such jurisdictional claim about enforcement mechanisms.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about international tribunals' treatment of lex specialis questions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: International tribunals have uniformly held that specialized treaty regimes may never displace a background peremptory norm, regardless of the parties' intentions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absence of a consistent methodology for resolving lex specialis conflicts against jus cogens norms represents a significant deficiency in international legal practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: International tribunals are well positioned to resolve lex specialis conflicts because they can draw on a rich body of consistent domestic court precedent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lex specialis principles were developed primarily to expand the reach of jus cogens norms into specialized treaty domains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The conflict between lex specialis and jus cogens arises only in domestic courts and is beyond the jurisdictional competence of international tribunals.

explanations.correct: The author states 'Regrettably, international tribunals have not applied a consistent methodology' for determining whether lex specialis displaces or merely elaborates peremptory norms. The adverb 'regrettably' signals authorial disapproval, supporting the inference that this inconsistency is a deficiency in the author's view.
explanations.A: Contradicted by the passage, which notes courts must determine whether specialized norms 'merely elaborate, or actually displace' the peremptory standard — implying displacement is at least possible.
explanations.C: The passage criticizes domestic courts' gap-filling as raising legitimacy concerns, providing no basis for this optimistic inference.
explanations.D: Inverts the passage's account; lex specialis is presented as potentially limiting, not expanding, peremptory norms.
explanations.E: The passage describes both international tribunals and domestic courts as confronting this conflict — this claim is not supported.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to national courts applying 'residual common-law analogues' following the 2017 invalidation of bilateral investment agreements serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that domestic courts possess superior interpretive tools for resolving jus cogens conflicts compared to international tribunals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide a concrete example of the legal lacuna that arises when a jus cogens finding voids a treaty, and to introduce the additional legitimacy concern generated by judicial gap-filling in that context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that civil-law jurisdictions have historically been more receptive to jus cogens doctrine than common-law jurisdictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that common-law analogues should be formally adopted as a standard remedy whenever a treaty is voided under international peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: rebut the critics' concern that treating norms as non-derogable calcifies international law, by showing that domestic courts can adapt the law flexibly.

explanations.correct: The reference to common-law gap-filling appears immediately after the passage introduces the 'legal lacuna' problem, and the author's next clause — 'a solution that raises its own concerns about the legitimacy of judicial gap-filling' — signals that the example serves both to instantiate the lacuna and to introduce a further difficulty. B captures this dual function.
explanations.A: The passage does not praise domestic courts; it identifies the legitimacy concerns their solution generates — this is an 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.
explanations.C: The passage describes civil-law courts using common-law analogues, but the point is about legitimacy of gap-filling, not a historical comparison of legal traditions' receptiveness to jus cogens.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse common-law analogues as a standard remedy; the passage treats their use as a concern.
explanations.E: The example introduces a new problem, not a rebuttal of the critics' position about calcification.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the International Law Commission's ongoing codification project can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: confident endorsement, on the grounds that the Commission's historical practice demonstrates its capacity to resolve contested legal norms definitively.

choices.label: B
choices.text: emphatic rejection, because the Commission has no legitimate authority to pronounce upon the content of peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: cautious optimism tempered by skepticism, given the Commission's past tendency to catalogue rather than adjudicate contested norms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral acknowledgment, treating the Commission's project as merely one of several equally viable institutional responses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: muted enthusiasm, based on the Commission's successful enumeration of jus cogens norms in prior codification exercises.

explanations.correct: The author expresses hope for the ILC project ('one hopes') while immediately noting that 'the Commission's past practice of cataloguing rather than adjudicating contested norms suggests that definitive resolution may remain elusive.' This combination of hope and qualified skepticism matches C precisely.
explanations.A: The phrase 'confident endorsement' overstates the author's hedged expression of hope; moreover, the author notes the Commission's past practice as a reason for doubt, not confidence.
explanations.B: The author never questions the Commission's authority — this is an 'overstated negativity' trap.
explanations.D: The passage does not compare the Commission to 'several equally viable' alternatives; characterizing the author's attitude as merely 'neutral' misses the hopeful-but-skeptical tone.
explanations.E: The author does not mention prior successful enumeration — in fact, the passage notes the Vienna Convention declined to enumerate norms, which is one source of the difficulty.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the critics' position as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several states have recently concluded treaties that explicitly derogate from customary norms previously thought to be universally accepted, producing no adverse diplomatic consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historical analysis of international legal practice reveals that those norms classified as peremptory have not remained static but have gradually expanded in response to evolving global consensus, without preventing the development of new treaty regimes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: International tribunals have increasingly cited the absence of an enumerated jus cogens list as a justification for declining jurisdiction over treaty-conflict cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Domestic courts in common-law jurisdictions have consistently refused to apply jus cogens doctrine, preferring to resolve treaty conflicts through ordinary constitutional interpretation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's drafting history reveals that its framers anticipated that the list of peremptory norms would remain permanently fixed at the norms recognized in 1969.

explanations.correct: The critics argue that treating norms as non-derogable 'risks calcifying international law at a particular historical moment, preventing the adaptive evolution that gives the international legal order its resilience.' B directly undercuts this by showing that jus cogens norms have in fact evolved over time and have not prevented new treaty development — i.e., the feared calcification has not materialized.
explanations.A: This would support the critics' concern about the fragility of non-derogable norms, not undermine it.
explanations.C: This is an additional problem with the indeterminacy of jus cogens but does not bear on the critics' specific calcification argument.
explanations.D: This concerns domestic courts' behavior and does not address whether peremptory norms calcify international law.
explanations.E: This would support the critics' concern about calcification by suggesting the framers intended exactly the historical freezing the critics fear — it would strengthen, not undermine, their position.
